        <header class="article-header">
            <div class="article-category"><i class="fas fa-bug"></i> Vulnerability Analysis</div>
            <h1>Microsoft Patch Tuesday January 2026: 114 CVEs, 3 Zero-Days, and One Actively Exploited</h1>
            <p class="article-excerpt">Microsoft kicks off 2026 with a massive security update addressing 114
                vulnerabilities including CVE-2026-20805, an information disclosure flaw in Windows DWM that
                attackers are already weaponizing in the wild.</p>
            <div class="article-meta">
                <span><i class="far fa-calendar-alt"></i> Released: January 14, 2026</span>
                <span><i class="fas fa-clock"></i> Published: Jan 16, 2026</span>
                <span><i class="fas fa-book-open"></i> 20 min read</span>
                <span><i class="fas fa-user"></i> By Harish G</span>
            </div>
        </header>

        <img src="/images/articles/microsoft-patch-tuesday-january-2026.png"
            alt="Microsoft Patch Tuesday January 2026 Analysis" class="featured-image" loading="lazy">

        <div class="stat-grid">
            <div class="stat-card">
                <span class="stat-value">114</span>
                <span class="stat-label">Total CVEs Patched</span>
            </div>
            <div class="stat-card">
                <span class="stat-value red">3</span>
                <span class="stat-label">Zero-Day Vulnerabilities</span>
            </div>
            <div class="stat-card">
                <span class="stat-value orange">8</span>
                <span class="stat-label">Critical Severity</span>
            </div>
            <div class="stat-card">
                <span class="stat-value purple">1</span>
                <span class="stat-label">Actively Exploited</span>
            </div>
        </div>

        <h2><i class="fas fa-crosshairs"></i> Executive Summary</h2>

        <p>Microsoft's first Patch Tuesday of 2026 is one for the record books. Released on January 14, 2026, this
            security update addresses <strong>114 vulnerabilities</strong> across the Windows ecosystem, including
            <strong>three zero-day vulnerabilities</strong>—one of which is confirmed to be actively exploited in
            the wild.</p>

        <p>The star of this month's update is <strong>CVE-2026-20805</strong>, an information disclosure
            vulnerability in Windows Desktop Window Manager (DWM) that threat actors are actively leveraging as part
            of exploit chains. Despite its moderate CVSS score of 5.5, its active exploitation status means security
            teams should treat this as a priority-one patch.</p>

        <p>Beyond the zero-days, this update includes eight critical-severity vulnerabilities affecting Microsoft
            Office, Windows LSASS, Windows NTFS, and the Graphics Component. Several of these enable remote code
            execution (RCE) through maliciously crafted files—a classic attack vector that continues to plague
            enterprise environments.</p>

        <div class="warning-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-exclamation-triangle"></i> Urgent Action Required:</strong> CVE-2026-20805 is
            actively exploited in the wild and has been added to CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV)
            catalog. Federal agencies must remediate by February 3, 2026. All organizations should patch
            immediately.
        </div>

        <h2><i class="fas fa-skull-crossbones"></i> The Actively Exploited Zero-Day: CVE-2026-20805</h2>

        <div class="cve-highlight">
            <span class="cve-id">CVE-2026-20805</span>
            <span class="cvss-score">CVSS 5.5</span>
            <span class="status-badge"><i class="fas fa-fire"></i> ACTIVELY EXPLOITED</span>
            <p style="margin-top: 1rem; color: var(--text-secondary);">Windows Desktop Window Manager (DWM)
                Information Disclosure Vulnerability</p>
        </div>

        <h3>What is CVE-2026-20805?</h3>

        <p>CVE-2026-20805 is an information disclosure vulnerability in the Windows Desktop Window Manager (DWM),
            the core Windows component responsible for desktop composition and visual effects. The vulnerability
            allows an attacker to leak kernel memory addresses—information that shouldn't be accessible to regular
            applications.</p>

        <p>You might wonder why a "mere" information disclosure bug warrants critical attention. The answer lies in
            how modern exploitation works. Attackers rarely use a single vulnerability—they chain multiple bugs
            together. Memory address leaks like CVE-2026-20805 are invaluable for bypassing Address Space Layout
            Randomization (ASLR), one of Windows' fundamental security defenses.</p>

        <h3>The Attack Chain</h3>

        <p>Security researchers have observed CVE-2026-20805 being used in a multi-stage attack chain:</p>

        <div class="timeline">
            <div class="timeline-item">
                <span class="timeline-date">Stage 1: Initial Access</span>
                <span class="timeline-event">Attacker delivers malicious document or tricks user into visiting
                    weaponized website</span>
            </div>
            <div class="timeline-item">
                <span class="timeline-date">Stage 2: Memory Leak (CVE-2026-20805)</span>
                <span class="timeline-event">Vulnerability exploited to leak kernel memory addresses, defeating
                    ASLR</span>
            </div>
            <div class="timeline-item">
                <span class="timeline-date">Stage 3: Privilege Escalation</span>
                <span class="timeline-event">Leaked addresses used to precisely target a kernel vulnerability for
                    SYSTEM privileges</span>
            </div>
            <div class="timeline-item">
                <span class="timeline-date">Stage 4: Persistence</span>
                <span class="timeline-event">Attacker establishes persistent access, deploys malware or
                    ransomware</span>
            </div>
        </div>

        <h3>Who is Exploiting CVE-2026-20805?</h3>

        <p>Microsoft has not publicly attributed the exploitation to a specific threat actor, but intelligence
            sources suggest the vulnerability is being used by both state-sponsored groups and financially motivated
            attackers. The broad utility of ASLR bypass techniques makes this vulnerability valuable to virtually
            any advanced threat actor.</p>

        <p>What's particularly concerning is the speed of exploitation. The vulnerability was being exploited before
            the patch was released (hence "zero-day"), indicating either:</p>

        <ul>
            <li>Independent discovery by threat actors</li>
            <li>Possible leak of vulnerability details</li>
            <li>Sophisticated research capabilities of the attacking group</li>
        </ul>

        <h2><i class="fas fa-shield-virus"></i> The Other Zero-Days</h2>

        <p>While CVE-2026-20805 gets the headlines for active exploitation, Microsoft patched two additional
            zero-day vulnerabilities that were publicly disclosed before the patch:</p>

        <h3>CVE-2023-31096: Agere Soft Modem Driver Privilege Escalation</h3>

        <table>
            <tr>
                <th>Property</th>
                <th>Value</th>
            </tr>
            <tr>
                <td>CVE ID</td>
                <td><code>CVE-2023-31096</code></td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
                <td>Type</td>
                <td>Elevation of Privilege</td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
                <td>Component</td>
                <td>Windows Agere Soft Modem Driver (agrsm64.sys / agrsm.sys)</td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
                <td>Resolution</td>
                <td>Affected drivers removed from Windows</td>
            </tr>
        </table>

        <p>This is an interesting case—the CVE was originally assigned by MITRE back in 2023, but it took until 2026
            for Microsoft to address it. The delay is due to the affected drivers being third-party components
            (LSI/Agere) that were bundled with Windows. Microsoft's resolution is definitive: they've simply removed
            the vulnerable drivers from the operating system entirely.</p>

        <h3>CVE-2026-21265: Secure Boot Security Feature Bypass</h3>

        <table>
            <tr>
                <th>Property</th>
                <th>Value</th>
            </tr>
            <tr>
                <td>CVE ID</td>
                <td><code>CVE-2026-21265</code></td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
                <td>CVSS Score</td>
                <td>6.4 (Medium)</td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
                <td>Type</td>
                <td>Security Feature Bypass</td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
                <td>Attack Vector</td>
                <td>Local, requires high privileges</td>
            </tr>
        </table>

        <p>CVE-2026-21265 is a Secure Boot bypass that could allow an authenticated attacker with high privileges to
            circumvent security features through weaknesses in the certificate update mechanism. While it requires
            local access and elevated privileges, Secure Boot bypasses are particularly valuable for attackers
            seeking to establish persistent, boot-level malware that survives system reinstallation.</p>

        <div class="info-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-key"></i> Key Takeaway:</strong> Secure Boot vulnerabilities are rare but
            impactful. If you're running environments where firmware integrity is critical (financial systems,
            critical infrastructure), prioritize this patch even though it's not rated critical.
        </div>

        <h2><i class="fas fa-bomb"></i> Critical Vulnerabilities: The Remote Code Execution Threats</h2>

        <p>Microsoft rated eight vulnerabilities as Critical in this release. Here are the ones security teams
            should focus on:</p>

        <h3>Microsoft Office RCE Vulnerabilities</h3>

        <table>
            <thead>
                <tr>
                    <th>CVE ID</th>
                    <th>Component</th>
                    <th>CVSS</th>
                    <th>Preview Pane?</th>
                </tr>
            </thead>
            <tbody>
                <tr>
                    <td><code>CVE-2026-20944</code></td>
                    <td>Microsoft Word</td>
                    <td><span class="severity-badge severity-critical">8.4</span></td>
                    <td>No</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><code>CVE-2026-20955</code></td>
                    <td>Microsoft Excel</td>
                    <td><span class="severity-badge severity-high">7.8</span></td>
                    <td>No</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><code>CVE-2026-20957</code></td>
                    <td>Microsoft Excel</td>
                    <td><span class="severity-badge severity-high">7.8</span></td>
                    <td>No</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><code>CVE-2026-20952</code></td>
                    <td>Microsoft Office</td>
                    <td><span class="severity-badge severity-critical">Critical</span></td>
                    <td><strong>Yes!</strong></td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><code>CVE-2026-20953</code></td>
                    <td>Microsoft Office</td>
                    <td><span class="severity-badge severity-critical">Critical</span></td>
                    <td><strong>Yes!</strong></td>
                </tr>
            </tbody>
        </table>

        <p>The most dangerous of these are CVE-2026-20952 and CVE-2026-20953. These Office vulnerabilities can be
            triggered through Outlook's Preview Pane—meaning a user doesn't even need to open the malicious
            attachment. Simply selecting the email in Outlook is enough to trigger exploitation.</p>

        <div class="warning-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-exclamation-triangle"></i> Critical Risk:</strong> CVE-2026-20952 and
            CVE-2026-20953 can be exploited through Outlook Preview Pane. Disable the Preview Pane immediately as a
            temporary mitigation until patches are deployed.
        </div>

        <h3>Windows LSASS Remote Code Execution</h3>

        <table>
            <tr>
                <th>CVE ID</th>
                <td><code>CVE-2026-20854</code></td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
                <th>Component</th>
                <td>Windows Local Security Authority Subsystem Service (LSASS)</td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
                <th>CVSS Score</th>
                <td><span class="severity-badge severity-high">7.5</span></td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
                <th>Attack Vector</th>
                <td>Network</td>
            </tr>
        </table>

        <p>LSASS is the heart of Windows authentication. It handles login validation, password changes, and security
            token creation. A remote code execution vulnerability in LSASS is particularly dangerous because:</p>

        <ul>
            <li>LSASS runs with SYSTEM privileges—the highest privilege level in Windows</li>
            <li>Successful exploitation gives attackers complete control over the target</li>
            <li>LSASS is network-accessible in domain environments</li>
            <li>Domain controllers running LSASS are high-value targets</li>
        </ul>

        <h3>Windows NTFS Heap Buffer Overflow</h3>

        <p>CVE-2026-20840 and CVE-2026-20922 are heap-based buffer overflow vulnerabilities in Windows NTFS, the
            primary filesystem for Windows. Both have a CVSS score of 7.8 and enable RCE when processing specially
            crafted disk images or mounted volumes.</p>

        <p>Attack scenarios include:</p>

        <ul>
            <li>User mounts a malicious USB drive</li>
            <li>User extracts a malicious ISO or VHD file</li>
            <li>Attacker tricks user into mounting a network share containing exploit</li>
        </ul>

        <h2><i class="fas fa-chart-bar"></i> Breakdown by Category</h2>

        <p>Let's look at the full distribution of vulnerabilities in this Patch Tuesday:</p>

        <table>
            <thead>
                <tr>
                    <th>Category</th>
                    <th>Count</th>
                    <th>Key Components</th>
                </tr>
            </thead>
            <tbody>
                <tr>
                    <td>Elevation of Privilege</td>
                    <td><strong>47</strong></td>
                    <td>Windows Kernel, DWM, VBS Enclave, RRAS</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>Remote Code Execution</td>
                    <td><strong>28</strong></td>
                    <td>Office, LSASS, NTFS, OLE</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>Information Disclosure</td>
                    <td><strong>17</strong></td>
                    <td>DWM (the zero-day), Windows Kernel</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>

                    <td><strong>12</strong></td>
                    <td>Various Windows services</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>Security Feature Bypass</td>

                    <td>Secure Boot, Windows Security</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>Spoofing</td>
                    <td><strong>2</strong></td>
                    <td>Windows components</td>
                </tr>
            </tbody>
        </table>

        <p>The high proportion of Elevation of Privilege vulnerabilities (47 out of 114) reflects the security
            research community's focus on local privilege escalation—a critical link in attack chains that convert
            initial access into full system compromise.</p>

        <p>January 2026 represents a <strong>58% increase</strong> in patched vulnerabilities compared to December
            2025, making it one of the largest Patch Tuesdays in recent memory. The three zero-days also tie for the
            most zero-days patched in a single month over the past year.</p>

        <h2><i class="fas fa-shield-alt"></i> Remediation and Mitigation Strategies</h2>

        <h3>Immediate Actions (Within 24-48 Hours)</h3>

        <div class="success-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-shield-alt"></i> Priority 1 - Do Now:</strong>
            <ul>
                <li><strong>Patch CVE-2026-20805</strong> on all Windows endpoints immediately—it's actively
                    exploited</li>
                <li><strong>Disable Outlook Preview Pane</strong> to mitigate CVE-2026-20952/20953 until patches are
                    deployed</li>
                <li><strong>Prioritize Domain Controllers</strong> for the LSASS vulnerability (CVE-2026-20854)</li>
                <li><strong>Block untrusted USB devices</strong> to mitigate NTFS vulnerabilities while patching
                </li>
            </ul>
        </div>

        <h3>Standard Patching Timeline</h3>

        <ul>
            <li><strong>Critical/Actively Exploited:</strong> 24-48 hours</li>
            <li><strong>Critical RCE:</strong> 7 days</li>
            <li><strong>High Severity:</strong> 14 days</li>
            <li><strong>Medium/Low:</strong> 30 days (standard patch cycle)</li>
        </ul>

        <h3>Detection and Hunting</h3>

        <p>While patching, security teams should hunt for signs of exploitation:</p>

        <ul>
            <li><strong>CVE-2026-20805:</strong> Monitor for unusual DWM.exe behavior, unexpected memory reads, or
                process injection attempts targeting dwm.exe</li>
            <li><strong>Office exploits:</strong> Watch for suspicious Office process spawning child processes
                (cmd.exe, powershell.exe, mshta.exe)</li>
            <li><strong>LSASS attacks:</strong> Enable Credential Guard if not already active; monitor LSASS for
                unusual network connections</li>
        </ul>

        <h2><i class="fas fa-building"></i> Impact on Different Industries</h2>

        <h3>Healthcare</h3>
        <p>Healthcare organizations should prioritize patching immediately. With the ransomware epidemic continuing
            to target hospitals, the combination of Office RCE vulnerabilities and the actively exploited DWM bug
            creates significant risk for clinical systems.</p>

        <h3>Financial Services</h3>
        <p>The Secure Boot bypass (CVE-2026-21265) is particularly relevant for financial institutions where boot
            integrity is a compliance requirement. Domain controllers running LSASS are also high-value targets that
            require immediate attention.</p>

        <h3>Critical Infrastructure</h3>
        <p>OT environments often have delayed patching cycles, but the active exploitation of CVE-2026-20805 means
            infrastructure operators should accelerate testing and deployment. Network segmentation between IT and
            OT remains critical.</p>

        <h3>Education</h3>
        <p>Educational institutions are frequent targets for ransomware. The Outlook Preview Pane vulnerabilities
            are particularly dangerous in environments where users may click on anything. Disable Preview Pane
            institution-wide as an immediate mitigation.</p>

        <h2><i class="fas fa-forward"></i> Future Implications</h2>

        <h3>The Exploit Chain Problem</h3>

        <p>CVE-2026-20805 illustrates a growing trend: attackers use multiple vulnerabilities together. A "moderate"
            information disclosure bug becomes critical when it enables ASLR bypass for a kernel exploit. Security
            teams need to evaluate vulnerabilities not just by CVSS score, but by their utility in attack chains.
        </p>

        <h3>Zero-Day Velocity</h3>

        <p>Three zero-days in one Patch Tuesday continues the trend of increased zero-day exploitation. Microsoft's
            own data shows zero-day exploitation has increased 50% year-over-year. Organizations need:</p>

        <ul>
            <li>Faster patching capabilities</li>
            <li>Better exploit detection (behavioral, not just signature-based)</li>
            <li>Reduce attack surface through principles like least privilege</li>
        </ul>

        <h3>The Preview Pane Continues to Haunt</h3>

        <p>Outlook's Preview Pane has been a source of zero-click vulnerabilities for years. CVE-2026-20952 and
            CVE-2026-20953 add to this legacy. Organizations should seriously consider disabling the Preview Pane by
            default—the convenience isn't worth the recurring security risk.</p>

        <h2><i class="fas fa-clipboard-list"></i> Key Takeaways</h2>

        <div class="info-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-key"></i> Summary:</strong>
            <ol>
                <li><strong>Patch CVE-2026-20805 immediately</strong>—it's actively exploited and added to CISA KEV
                </li>
                <li><strong>Disable Outlook Preview Pane</strong> to mitigate two critical Office RCE bugs</li>
                <li><strong>Prioritize Domain Controllers</strong> for the LSASS vulnerability</li>
                <li><strong>Block untrusted removable media</strong> while patching NTFS vulnerabilities</li>
                <li><strong>114 total vulnerabilities</strong> means thorough testing is essential—but don't let
                    that delay critical patches</li>
                <li><strong>Hunt for exploitation</strong> of the actively exploited zero-day in your environment
                </li>
            </ol>
        </div>
